variants.answer: Server rendering means the server builds the page’s HTML for each request and sends it ready to display; browser rendering means the browser downloads JavaScript and builds much or all of the page there. For a product page, I’d choose server rendering when search visibility and a fast first view matter—especially for public product listings. In a fictional project, I moved product details and key metadata into server-rendered HTML, then kept filters interactive in the browser. Our measured median time to useful product content fell from 2.4 to 1.6 seconds, while search impressions rose 12% over the following quarter. I’d lean toward browser rendering for highly interactive, personalized views where SEO is less important, such as an authenticated product configurator, provided the initial loading experience remains acceptable.

variants.answer: Server rendering sends HTML that the server has already generated, while browser rendering relies more on JavaScript running on the user’s device to create the page. For a public product page, I’d generally favor server rendering for quicker initial content and search indexing, then use browser code for interactions like selecting a size. For an internal or personalized product tool, browser rendering might be a better fit.
